heading.en: Integrals you can do without integrating

hook.en: Some *definite integrals* have no simple antiderivative, yet their value is easy: ∫₀^(π/2) log(tan x) dx is exactly 0. Symmetry does the work.
hook.kn: ಕೆಲವು ನಿಶ್ಚಿತ ಸಮಾಕಲನಗಳಿಗೆ ಸರಳ ಪ್ರತಿ-ಅವಕಲಜ ಇಲ್ಲ, ಆದರೂ ಬೆಲೆ ಸುಲಭ: ∫₀^(π/2) log(tan x) dx = 0. ಸಮಮಿತಿ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ.

body.en: $\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f$; $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$; $\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx$. The last two let us add an integral to its reflected copy.

body.en: $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$ if $f$ is even ($f(-x) = f(x)$), and $= 0$ if $f$ is odd ($f(-x) = -f(x)$). Also $\int_0^{2a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$ if $f(2a - x) = f(x)$, and 0 if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$.

tagline.en: The properties that make hard definite integrals easy: reversing limits, splitting the interval, f(a + b − x), f(2a − x), and even and odd functions.

myth.en: $\int_{-1}^{1} (x^2 + x)\,dx = 0$, because the interval is symmetric.

truth.en: Only the odd part vanishes. $\int_{-1}^1 x\,dx = 0$ but $\int_{-1}^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{2}{3}$, so the answer is $\frac{2}{3}$. A symmetric interval alone proves nothing; the function must be odd. $x^2 + x$ is neither even nor odd, so split it into its even and odd parts first.

say.en: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$; add the two forms when the integrand "swaps".
Split the interval wherever a modulus or greatest-integer function changes form.
$\int_{-a}^a f = 0$ for odd $f$ and $2\int_0^a f$ for even $f$.
$\int_0^{2a} f = 2\int_0^a f$ if $f(2a - x) = f(x)$, and 0 if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$.

goal.en: The properties that make hard definite integrals easy: reversing limits, splitting the interval, f(a + b − x), f(2a − x), and even and odd functions.

takeaway.en: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$; add the two forms when the integrand "swaps".

narration.en: Many people think: $\int_{-1}^{1} (x^2 + x)\,dx = 0$, because the interval is symmetric. Actually: Only the odd part vanishes. $\int_{-1}^1 x\,dx = 0$ but $\int_{-1}^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{2}{3}$, so the answer is $\frac{2}{3}$. A symmetric interval alone proves nothing; the function must be odd. $x^2 + x$ is neither even nor odd, so split it into its even and odd parts first.

problem.en: Evaluate I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx.

steps.en: Using f(π/2 − x): I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Evaluate I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Evaluate I equals the integral of 0^(pi /2) sin x over sin x plus cos x dx.
Using f(pi /2 - x): I equals the integral of 0^(pi /2) cos x over cos x plus sin x dx.
Add: 2I equals the integral of 0^(pi /2) 1 dx equals pi /2.
So the answer is pi /4.

steps.en: Each part is a triangle of base 3 and height 3: area 9/2.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Evaluate ∫₂⁸ |x − 5| dx.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Evaluate the integral of 2 to the power 8 |x minus 5| dx.
Split at 5: the integral of 2 to the power 5 (5 - x) dx plus the integral of 5 to the power 8 x minus 5 dx.
Each part is a triangle of base 3 and height 3: area 9 over 2.
So the answer is 9.

body.en: Whenever the integrand changes into a "partner" under x → a + b − x (sin ↔ cos on [0, π/2], x ↔ a − x), write I both ways and add. The awkward part usually becomes 1, and the answer is half the length of the interval.

narration.en: King's property. Whenever the integrand changes into a "partner" under x → a + b − x (sin ↔ cos on [0, π/2], x ↔ a − x), write I both ways and add. The awkward part usually becomes 1, and the answer is half the length of the interval.

say.en: King's property. Whenever the integrand changes into a "partner" under x gives a plus b - x (sin ↔ cos on [0, pi /2], x ↔ a - x), write I both ways and add. The awkward part usually becomes 1, and the answer is half the length of the interval.
